title: The Man Who Kept the Air
passages:
Wren's lamp beam caught the other light at thirty meters, a pale smear in the green water that didn't bob like a diver's. She stopped kicking, let the current hold her against the stairwell railing, and waited for the shape to resolve. The tower groaned around them, a deep steel cough that vibrated through her boots and into her teeth.

The light came from a helmet mounted on a suit patched so many times the original color was a guess. Salt crust glazed the seams, stiff as barnacles. One fin was missing, the other held on by a loop of orange twine — same whipping twine she carried in her thigh pocket. A paint marker dangled on a lanyard from the chest D-ring. The man's right leg hung at an angle that made her stomach turn, the knee swollen purple-black against the neoprene. He didn't kick. He didn't need to. He was anchored to a handrail by a carabiner, drifting like a buoy.

He raised a gloved hand and tapped her lamp twice. *Tap-tap.* The old divers' *I see you.* She tapped back, once, *I see you too.*

He didn't speak. Didn't offer a name. Instead he extended his left wrist, the slate mounted there glowing faint numbers through the grime. She swam closer, close enough to taste the metal in the water, and read.

Depth: 42m. Time at depth: 371 days. Air pressure: 1.2 bar. Pulse: 48 bpm. Scrubber cycles: 14,600. Memory logs: 0.

Three hundred seventy-one days. A year and six days. The pulse was steady, the air pressure holding, the scrubber count climbing like a clock. But the memory logs — the buffer that recorded what a diver saw, heard, thought — sat at zero. Not corrupted. Not erased. Zero. As if the slate had never been asked to store a single moment.

Wren's fingers found the edge of her own slate pouch. Her slate, the one she'd built last night, showed an eleven-second cut she didn't remember making — matching the cut she'd put in Sol's record — and nine minutes unaccounted for in her deck log, a gap no backup could explain. And now this man, this *Salas* if the voice on the backup band was his, had spent over a year at the depth where memory goes to die, and his slate said he hadn't kept a single one.

He tapped the slate again, harder. *Read it,* the gesture said. *Know what you're looking at.*

She read it again. The numbers didn't lie. Slates didn't lie. They recorded what the body knew: pressure, time, gas mix, heartbeats. The memory log was optional, a choice a diver made before descent — *record* or *don't*. Most chose *record*. The deep took the memories anyway, but the slate kept a copy topside. Wren's job was to stitch those copies back into something a diver could live with.

Salas had chosen *don't*. For three hundred seventy-one days.

His helmet lights swung to her faceplate. Behind the scratched acrylic, eyes watched her, pale and clear in the green. He didn't blink. He waited for her to say something, to ask the question he'd made her read the answer to.

She keyed her push-to-talk. "Three hundred seventy-one days," she said. Her voice sounded thin in her own ears. "You've been down here a year."

He didn't nod. Didn't shake his head. He just pointed down the corridor, past the pharmacy pod she'd just unsealed, toward the darker water where the ward ceiling trapped a pocket of air. Then he tapped his throat — *talk* — and made a slow circle with one finger: *all of it.*

She exhaled, long and slow, watching bubbles climb. "Okay," she said. "Show me."

Salas didn't wait. He unclipped his carabiner, braced a boot against the corroded stair rail, and pulled himself hand-over-hand down the corridor, the motion smooth as a man walking a hallway. Wren followed, finning slow to keep the silt down, her lamp beam trembling over walls that had once been white tile. Now they were green-black with growth, the grout eaten away, the steel ribs of the building showing through like bones.

The corridor opened into a wider space — a maintenance ward, she guessed, by the rows of empty brackets where equipment had hung. The ceiling here was lower, a concrete slab that had trapped a pocket of air when the tower flooded. The waterline ran horizontal across the walls, a sharp, greasy mark at chest height on her. Above it, the air pocket breathed. She could hear it: a slow, wet suction as the tower settled, the air compressing and expanding in the dark.

Salas hauled himself up onto a rusted cabinet bolted to the wall, his bad leg trailing useless, and broke the surface with a sound like a seal surfacing. His helmet lights cut the gloom. Wren rose beside him, her suit's buoyancy compensator clicking as she vented, and lifted her head into the pocket.

The air tasted of old oil, salt, and something sweet-sick — acetone, maybe, or the ghost of medicines long gone. The ceiling was low, forcing a crouch. Paint tallies marched across the steel beams in silver marker: groups of five, over and over, three hundred seventy-one marks by her count. Each cluster had a date scratched beside it in a cramped hand. The earliest was faded to a ghost; the freshest, yesterday's, still bright.

A nest of mattress foam and thermal blankets huddled in the corner, compressed flat by a year of weight. Empty scrubber canisters — soda-lime cartridges, the kind that strip carbon dioxide from rebreathed air — stood ranked along a shelf like bottles in a pantry. Fourteen, six hundred, she thought, matching the slate. Four a day, give or take. He'd rationed them to the hour.

Salas floated beside the shelf, one hand on a beam, breathing loud in the small space. He didn't look at the tallies. He pointed his lamp at the steel bulkhead behind the foam.

Wren swam closer, her gloves brushing the damp insulation. The paint marker had bled into the metal, the letters jagged and hurried, as if written by a hand that shook or a mind that knew it wouldn't get a second chance.

*WREN ACHEBE. BRING THE WINCH. SAY IT THREE TIMES.*

Her name. Her full name, the one she used on manifests and contracts. Not *Wren*. Not *Reader*. *Wren Achebe.*

The backup channel hissed in her ear — Nia's pencil scratching, Sol's ratchet breathing, the storm hammering the hull. And underneath it all, the voice that had called her name for months: *Wren. Wren Achebe. Bring the winch.*

She pressed her fingers to the letters. The paint was dry, the edges crisp. No salt crust over them — written after the pocket formed, after the water rose. Written from inside the air pocket, by someone who had stood here, in this air, and known she would come.

Her throat closed. She keyed her mic. "It was me," she said, the words thin in the pocket's dead air. "I wrote this. I came down here before. I told you my name."

Salas hovered, his pale eyes on her face through the scratched acrylic. He didn't nod. He didn't need to. The tallies, the canisters, the foam nest — all of it said the same thing: he had waited. A year and six days. And she had promised.

Salas didn't answer the promise. He started talking instead, fast, like a man trying to outrun something.

"The tower was already going when I got there," he said. "Mercy General, pediatrics, fourth floor. West pilings had let go and the whole wing was leaning — this slow roll you feel in the deck before you hear it." He stopped. His eyes went flat and far. "I was down there because—"

He turned his lamp to the wall, to the tallies, and read them the way a man finds his place in a book he's dropped. His lips moved. Then his face cleared and he picked the thread back up.

"The capsule. Two of them in the peds bay. They seal themselves when there's living bodies inside — read the heat, the CO2, a heartbeat, all three, and weld the seam so nothing gets in or out till somebody cuts it open. I put the boy in first. Then the girl, and she fought me the whole way, bit through my glove, because she thought I was—" He lost it again. Found it on the wall. "Because she had no reason to trust a man in a dive suit zipping her brother into a box."

"You put them out the window," Wren said.

"East side. Water was already at the sill. It floats — that's the whole idea, it's built to be found." His breath fogged the acrylic. "I told myself somebody would find it."

"Somebody did."

He looked at her like he'd forgotten she was in the room. "Who are you?"

The question sat wrong in her chest, but she'd been ready for it since the slate read zero. She keyed the band to topside. "Nia. You at the table?"

"Here." Small through the static, the scrape of grease pencil behind it. "Storm's got the hull. Talk fast."

"I need the cold-case. The capsule we raised. Read me the number on it, and the band they sealed in with the kids."

"Case four-four-nine-bravo. Mercy General, peds, sealed capsule, recovered with two minors inside." No hesitation. "ID band reads the same — I copied it myself. Nobody edits the pencil."

*Nobody edits the pencil.* Wren let it sit.

She turned to Salas. "Four-four-nine-bravo. Two kids. A boy and a girl. Sealed in a capsule and shoved out an east window to float." She watched his eyes come back from wherever the deep keeps them. "That's your case. That's the one you sent up."

He read the wall again, and this time his finger stopped on the fresh paint, yesterday's date, and something in his shoulders let go like a knot worked loose.

"The girl on your radio," he said slowly. "The one writing it all down. Who is she?"

And Wren, who rebuilds what people are allowed to remember for a living, who has spent years deciding which hours a person gets to keep, heard herself hand the truth over whole.

"The one you floated."

Salas's face did a slow, complicated thing and settled on nothing.

"Then she's still got the pencil," he said. "Good. Somebody should."

He dug into his thigh pocket and came out with a coil of orange whipping twine wound on a paint stirrer — waxed line, the stuff you bind a rope end with so the strands don't work loose in the cold. He held it up like a man showing a badge.

"Rule's mine. I made it the second week, when I still had the head for it." He pinched off a length and tied it round the beam in front of her, three turns and a tuck, tail left hanging long. "Three turns and a tuck on the pod's seal ring, tail long. That means there's live ones sealed inside and the girl with the pencil gets told to send the drum down." He pulled the tail free and cut the ends flush with his thumbnail. "Cut ends, no tail. Means it went up without me. Don't wait, don't come looking, don't spend air on a promise."

"And who ties it?"

"Whoever's got hands." He coiled the line again. "It worked, didn't it. You're standing in my living room."

"It's a closet."

"It's a *dry* closet."

Wren let that go. The pocket sucked in and let go, sucked in and let go, and the paint tallies caught her lamp every time the beam swung.

"The second dive was for the boy," Salas said. "His course. Cartridges, sealed in a dispensary case, third shelf, and I knew the shelf because I stacked it myself before the west pilings let go. I went down for it." His finger found a date on the beam and stopped there. "Surge took the stair door off the top hinge and laid it across my ankle. Steel. Eighty kilos if it's a gram. Fire door — it shuts itself, that's the whole job, it doesn't check first." He said it the way another man would read a gauge. "Day and a bit. I got out by cutting the boot off and leaving the foot in it. Marked every canister on that shelf with a stroke of paint so I'd know which ones I'd already breathed. You count your own air or the air counts you."

"You went back down on that leg."

"The boy needed the medicine." He looked at her as if she'd asked why he'd bothered to breathe.

"Why zero?" Wren said. "Memory logs, zero. Nobody does that. The slate keeps a copy topside even when the deep takes the day out of you — that's the copy I work from, that's the whole job, I stitch people back together out of what their body wrote down."

"That's why." He said it flat. "You lose the afternoon down here, fine. But a copy means somebody up top with a pencil decides which afternoon you get handed back. I didn't want a year of me sitting in a drawer where a stranger could pick through it and give me the parts he liked."

Wren, who had done exactly that on a Thursday for money, found the ceiling very interesting.

"Cost you anything?"

"Nobody can vouch for me," he said. "I can't prove I zipped two kids in a box. Can't prove I came back for the medicine. Girl with the pencil's the only record there is, and she was four floors up in the dark." He shrugged the working shoulder. "Cheap."

"Last night," Wren said. "You said a diver came down."

"One came down the stairwell with a slate she'd built herself — I know the housing, I've seen factory, that wasn't factory — and a gauge reading her nine minutes, and no spare. I had a good canister on that shelf. Soda lime, sealed, forty cycles in it." His jaw worked. "She didn't want it. I put it in her housing and shut the collar on her fingers so she couldn't hand it back. Made her say she'd bring the winch. Made her say it three times, then I wrote it on the steel, because I lose things."

"Who'd you give it to?"

"Diver. Homemade slate. Bad gauge." He tipped his lamp at the shelf, at the long ranks of empties standing like stock in a pantry. "That was the last one that wasn't already breathed."

Wren's hand went to the collar at her chest, and stayed there, and she did not turn the latch.

Wren keyed her mic. "Topside, you copy?"

"Copy." Sol's voice came through tight, the ratchet's click-clack under every word. "Air?"

Wren glanced at her gauge — eighteen minutes at current burn, less if she worked — then at Salas's slate still strapped to his wrist. Scrubber cycles frozen at 14,600. The shelf behind him held nothing but empties ranked like clean bones. No fresh canisters. Her own suit was the only gas in the pocket.

"Eighteen minutes on my bottle," she said. "No spare. Shelf's empty. His scrubber's dead."

Static. Then Sol: "Cracking the last bottle. Wide open."

Wren heard the hiss over the band — high, sharp, the sound of a regulator pouring gas into a hungry line. Then a lower note, the *clack-clack-clack* of ice forming in the first stage. Frost on the diaphragm. The needle on the panel gauge screaming into the red.

"Regulator's frosting," Sol said. Calm. Too calm. "Needle's in the red. We buy minutes or we don't."

"Sol." Nia's voice didn't rise. "Dey's breathing changed. Shallow. Longer pauses. He's not just asleep."

The ratchet stopped clicking. In the silence, Wren heard the storm hit the hull again, a full-body blow that made the tower shiver around them. Dust fell from the ceiling beams, silvering the paint tallies.

"Medicine comes up," Sol said over the band, the ratchet resuming its rhythm, slower now, heavier. "Or the line gets cut. That's the rule. You know the rule."

Wren looked at Salas. His pale eyes watched her through the scratched acrylic. He knew the arithmetic. He'd lived it for three hundred seventy-one days. The orange twine stayed coiled in his gloved hand, the paint stirrer tucked under his thumb.

"Copy," she said. "Medicine comes up. Or the line gets cut."

He unclipped the carabiner before she'd finished saying it.

The gate swung off the rail with a small bright click and he pushed off — one long pull of the arms, good boot braced, bad leg trailing behind him like something he'd forgotten to bring. He tapped his chest on the way past, then his mouthpiece. *My air. My hands. Don't argue.*

"No," Wren said, and got two fistfuls of harness webbing.

He was heavier than a man that thin had any right to be. Steel bottle, lead, a year of wet neoprene holding water, and a body that had decided some while back that being told no was just weather. He caught the door frame and started hauling. She got a boot against the rusted cabinet and hauled back, and for four or five seconds the two of them went nowhere at all in a room the size of a coffin stood on end.

"Let go."

"You're on a dead scrubber."

"I know what I'm on. I counted it." Another inch. "You've got fourteen minutes and you're spending them on me."

"Fourteen and change. And you can't carry two cases on one fin and a leg somebody cut out of a boot."

"I've carried worse."

"Not tonight."

He swore at her then, low and flat, the kind of swearing worn smooth from use. She swore back, most of it her mother's. His lamp knocked the wall and the beam went skating over the ranks of empties on the shelf.

Then she let go of him with her left hand, dug in her thigh pocket, and came up with the coil.

Plain orange whipping twine, no stirrer, no notch, just a hank wound tight and stowed the way you stow anything you might need in the dark. Three turns round the handrail, through the D-ring at the back of his harness, a tuck, tail left hanging long.

Salas stopped pulling. He watched her hands do it.

"You know what that says," he said.

"It says there's a live one sealed in here and the girl with the pencil gets told to send the drum down."

"Say the rest."

She pulled the tail snug. "I'm telling her."

Over the band, small and steady, Nia's grease pencil going: "Say your air out loud when it changes."

"Fourteen and change," Wren said.

Salas hung on the rail in his lashing and didn't fight it, which was worse than if he had. A man who stops fighting has finished the sum.

"Who taught you that knot?"

"Nobody. I read it off the wall."

"No." He turned his wrist so the light fell flat on his own hand, on the empty loop of line he'd coiled and put away five minutes ago. "I made that knot the second week, when I still had the head for it. Three turns and a tuck, tail long. I only ever taught it to one person, and she's not got the manners to remember."

The ward shifted. Not the breathing this time — a settle, the whole steel frame dropping a hand's width somewhere far off, and the trapped air squeezed up hard against the slab, so the pocket got smaller around them by a foot in every direction. Wren's shoulders came down. Salas's knees came up. Neither of them had room to be angry properly anymore.

"Say it," he said.

"I don't know what I said."

"Say it anyway. Out loud, for the pencil."

Wren looked at the tail of her own knot turning slowly in the water, and heard her voice on last night's traffic saying it in a room she has no record of standing in.

"I'll bring the winch."

"That's three," Salas said.

She had said it once. She knew she had said it once, tonight, in this room, ninety seconds ago, because she'd been there for it.

"That's not—" she started.

"Three turns and a tuck, said three times." He settled against the rail as far as the twine let him, one hand closing over it, testing, the way a man checks a hitch he's tied ten thousand times. "Then the drum comes down. That's the rule and I don't take it back for anybody's face."

"Sol," Wren said, and her voice came out wrong. "Say something."

The band gave her the ratchet, click-clack, slower and heavier than before. Then Sol, very calm: "I'm here. Keep your air."

Salas's lamp had drifted off her and down, past the cabinet, past the lip of the ward floor where the corridor fell away into the stairwell. He wasn't pointing it anywhere in particular. He wasn't looking at her at all.

"That's three," he said again, to nobody, almost kindly. "Now watch where I put the light."

The lamp went down.

Not on her. Past her, over the lip of the ward floor, down the throat of the stairwell where the green went to a color she had no name for. The beam fell in a long cone, catching silt, catching the bent rail of a landing, going down and down until it found a shape and stopped and held it.

A steel door hung open on one hinge. Above it a sign eaten to lace, the snake and the staff still legible. And against the far wall, squared up in a neat row by a man with more patience than sense, two white cases. Latched. Sealed. A boy's course stenciled across the lids in numbers she read twice, because she already knew them.

"Forty-nine," Salas said. "Dispensary landing. Surge put them there. I stacked that shelf myself before the wing went over."

Wren had the gauge in her fist before she'd decided to look. She knew the number. She said it anyway, out loud, flat, for the pencil.

"Depth, forty-two. Suit's rated to forty-two. Cases at forty-nine." She made herself finish it. "Seven meters past what this suit is built to hold. And at forty-nine there's near six atmospheres of water sitting on you, so one breath down there costs six times the gas of the same breath up here."

The grease pencil scratched. Nia didn't comment. She just kept the line open so Wren could hear her writing it down.

"Both cases. Down seven, rig them, lash them to the cable, back up seven, then the whole ascent from here with a stop for the bends. That's twenty-two minutes of gas. I have twelve." Her exhaust climbed past his faceplate and broke apart in the pocket. "One case is most of that same trip. The going is the cost, not the weight. And one case isn't a course. Half a course keeps nobody alive."

Twelve against twenty-two. It sat there in the dead air and didn't improve on inspection.

For years the job had been deciding which hour a person got handed back. She'd cut eleven seconds out of Sol on a Thursday and called it mercy, and Sol had gone up peaceful and short an hour. There was no blade for this. The deep didn't care what you wanted, and the only place on the boat to set a number like this down was in front of a girl with a pencil who wrote what happened and nothing else.

So she said it again, slower, so it would read clean if anybody ever went looking.

"Forty-nine meters. Seven past rating. Twelve minutes, no spare. Not enough to bring both up and live." A breath. "Not enough to bring one and live."

"There," Salas said. "Now it's written somewhere you can't get at with a knife."

She looked down at her own hands. The tail of the knot still turned slow in the water, three turns and a tuck, and the hank in her thigh pocket was the same orange, the same wax, the same lay in the strands.

She pulled it out and held it up. "Where did I get this?"

He tipped his lamp at the stirrer under his thumb, at the coil on it. One end was cut fresh, pale, no salt on it yet.

"Off me," he said. "Last night. You had a knife and I had one fin. I let you."

So that was who the mark was for. Not a stranger. A man on a rail with a dead scrubber and a wall to write on, and a woman who came down once with a homemade slate and no spare, cut a length off his line, and left him a hitch he'd taught her in a week she can't account for.

"I don't remember cutting it."

"You will or you won't." He settled against the lashing, testing the tail with two fingers, the way a man checks a hitch he's tied ten thousand times. "Doesn't change what's tied."

The ward drew in and let go. The pocket came down another hand's width and her shoulders found the slab, and the beam of her lamp lit the whole of it at once: two cases at forty-nine, twelve minutes on her wrist, one man breathing beside her who'd spent his last canister buying her the descent.

She was listening for one sound. It hadn't come yet.
